poems.text: Whoso, look you, thinks that his neighbour knows nothing, but that he himself alone possesses intricate counsels, he, I wot, is senseless, reft of sound mind: for we all are acquainted equally with crafty counsels. But one chooses not to follow filthy lucre, whilst to another faithless wile-weavings are more agreeable.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Now no limit of wealth
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Now no limit of wealth has been made-clear to men, for they who of us now have most substance, strive after twice as much. Who could satisfy all? Riches verily to mortals become folly. And from it up-starts ruin, which when Jove shall send upon them worn-and-weary, one at one time and another at another possesses.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Though he be citadel and
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Though he be citadel and tower to an empty-minded populace, Cyrnus, the noble man gets little share of praise. Nor longer, I wot, becomes it us, as men in a state of safety, to destroy, as it were, the walls of a city about to be taken.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: To thee indeed I have
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: To thee indeed I have given wings, wherewith thou wilt fly over boundless deep, and all earth, easily borne-aloft; and thou wilt be present at all banquets and feasts, resting in the mouths of many; thee too with sweet-voiced pipes young men gracefully lovely shall sing well and tunefully; and whensoe’er thou comest to the much-lamenting homes of Hades, beneath earth’s murky vaults, never more, even though dead, shalt thou lose thy renown, nor, I ween, escape notice, having ever imperishable fame among men, O Cyrnus, whilst thou tarriest in the land of Greece, or up and down the isles, crossing over the fishy barren deep, and not seated on the backs of horses; but, the tasteful gifts of violet-wreathed Muses will convey thee, for with all, to whom, even among posterity, minstrelsy is a care, thou wilt be likewise, as long as there shall be earth and sun. I, however, meet with small reverence from thee, but with words thou deceivest me, as a little child. That which is most just is most noble; health most preferable; but the gaining the object of one’s love is the most pleasant thing.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I am as it were
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I am as it were a well-bred racing mare, but I carry a very mean man: and this to me is most vexatious. Often ere now have I been ready to burst the bridle and flee, having thrust from me my mean charioteer.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Wine is not drunk by
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Wine is not drunk by me, since with a tender maiden, another man, far meaner than I, has the upper hand. Cold water to my sorrow her dear parents drink with her, so that she at the same time fetches water and bears me groaningly. Then having clasped the damsel round, I kissed her neck, and she spake tenderly with her lips.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Known, look you, is poverty
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Known, look you, is poverty, even though it be strange, for it neither comes to the market nor the law-suits. For everywhere it has the lesser share, and everywhere ’tis mocked: everywhere also, wheresoever it may be, it is equally hostile.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Equally, in truth, to mortal
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Equally, in truth, to mortal men the gods have given the other things, to wit, wretched old age and youth. But ’tis the worst of all the evils among men, and more unlucky than death and all diseases, after that you have reared children, and afforded them all things suitable, and laid up money for them, having experienced much trouble, if they hate their father, and pray that he may perish, and abhor him as if he were a beggar coming to them.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: It is likely that a
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: It is likely that a mean man would ill respect the rules of justice, since he stands-in-awe-of no divine-vengeance hereafter. For a worthless mortal may take up many impracticable things at the moment, and deem that he arranges all well.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Relying on none of the
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Relying on none of the citizens, advance one step, trusting neither oath nor covenant, not even if a man, wishing to give pledges, chooses to give Jove, the supreme king of immortals, as his surety. For verily in a city so malignantly-blaming as this, nothing pleases, and according as any one does, so they are called far the more senseless. But now the ills of the well-born are good things to the mean of men, and become a law to the devious. For a sense-of-shame hath perished: impudence and insolence, having mastered justice, possess the whole earth.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Neither does a lion always
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Neither does a lion always feast on flesh: but him, strong though he be, yet nevertheless perplexity seizes.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: To a babbling man silence
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: To a babbling man silence is the hardest burden, but an unlearned man, if he speak, is so to all in whose presence he may be. All hate him: yet the mixing up of such a man in a banquet is necessary. Nor does he wish to be a friend, when ill has chanced to a man, even though he may have been born of one and the same womb. Be bitter and sweet, harsh and kind, to hired servants and slaves and neighbours near-your-doors. It is not meet often-to-change a good life, but to keep peace: and to alter the ill life, until you have brought it right. The mean are not wholly mean from the womb, but through having cemented a friendship with mean men. And they have learned worthless works, and slanderous words, and insolence, supposing that all was true which those men said.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Among companions-at-a-meal, be a prudent
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Among companions-at-a-meal, be a prudent man; and deem that all escapes his notice, as if absent. Know how to endure jokes, and be brave out-of-doors, understanding what temper each has.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Among the mad indeed I
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Among the mad indeed I am exceeding mad; but among the just I am of all men most just.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Many mean men are rich
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Many mean men are rich, look you; and noble men are poor, yet with these we will not exchange their wealth for our excellence: for the latter is ever secure, but riches now one and now another of men possesses.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Cyrnus, a noble man hath
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Cyrnus, a noble man hath a judgment always firm, and is bold when set amidst blessings and amidst ills. But if the god shall present to a mean man substance and wealth, in-his-folly he is unable to contain his meanness.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Do not ever on a
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Do not ever on a slight pretext ruin a man that is a friend, trusting, Cyrnus, to a harsh slander. If a man in every instance should be wrath at the faults of his friends, never would men be in-concord or in-friendship one with the other. For faults follow-after mortal men, Cyrnus: but the gods choose not to endure them.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Even the slow man with-good-counsel
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Even the slow man with-good-counsel hath caught the swift man in the pursuit, Cyrnus, with the aid of the straight-forward justice of the immortal gods.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Quietly, as I do, pursue
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Quietly, as I do, pursue the middle way with thy feet, nor give to one party the property of the other, O Cyrnus.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Never, Cyrnus, kindly-treat an exile
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Never, Cyrnus, kindly-treat an exile on the ground of hope, for not even, if he has returned home, does he become any more the same.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Make-too-much haste in nothing, the
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Make-too-much haste in nothing, the mean is best of all: and thus, Cyrnus, thou shalt have excellence, which too it is hard to get.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: May Jove grant me both
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: May Jove grant me both requital of my friends, who love me, and that I may be more powerful than my foes. And so should I have the character of being a god among men, if the fate of death should overtake me, when I had recompensed them. But, O Jove, accomplish me, thou Olympian god, a seasonable prayer, grant me to experience in return for ills some good also. But oh might I die, unless I find some cessation from evil cares, and if thou givest but sorrows in return for sorrows. For thus is my lot; and there does not appear to me a means of vengeance on the men who perforce have plundered and possess my property; but like a dog I have crossed a mountain-torrent, having shaken off everything in the rain-swollen stream. Whose black blood may it be mine to drink: and oh might the good Genius aid me, who would accomplish these things to my mind.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: O worthless poverty, why tarriest
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: O worthless poverty, why tarriest thou, failing to go to another man? and why, prithee, dost love me, not desiring it? Nay, go; and visit another house, nor along with us be ever sharing this wretched life.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Be of good courage, Cyrnus
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Be of good courage, Cyrnus, in ills, for amid blessings too thou wast wont to rejoice, when the lot fell to thee to have a share of these too. And even as thou hast received ill out of blessings, even so also, praying to the gods, try to emerge again. Neither display it too much: for when exhibiting any ill, O Cyrnus, you have but few carers for your calamity.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: The heart of a man
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: The heart of a man, look you, O Cyrnus, having suffered great loss, is weakened; but when he takes vengeance, afterwards it is increased.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Beguile your enemy with good
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Beguile your enemy with good words: but when he shall have come into your power, take vengeance on him, having admitted of no excuse.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Restrain thy mind, and let
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Restrain thy mind, and let mildness ever attend thy tongue: the heart, look you, of mean men is more sharp than is meet.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I cannot understand the mind
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I cannot understand the mind of the citizens, which they entertain: for neither if I do them good, nor ill, do I please them: and many blame me, alike the base-born and the well-born: but none of the unwise can imitate me.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Do not, goading me perforce
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Do not, goading me perforce, and against my will, drive me under the waggon’s yoke, drawing me, Cyrnus, too much into friendship.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Kind Jove, I marvel at
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Kind Jove, I marvel at thee, for thou rulest over all, having honour thyself and vast power. Well knowest thou the mind of men, and the spirit of each; and thy might, O king, is highest of all. How is then, O son of Saturn, that thy purpose has-the-heart to hold men that are sinners, and the just man, in the same portion, both if thy mind shall have been turned towards moderation, and if towards the insolence of men yielding to unjust deeds? Neither is anything defined by the deity for mortals, nor the way in which walking a man may please the immortals. But nevertheless they hold wealth harmless; while they who keep their mind aloof from worthless deeds, still are-wont-to-find the mother of poverty, want-of-means, though they love what is just; want-of-means, which leads on the spirit of men to error, hurting their minds within their bosoms by strong necessity. So a man has-the-courage, though he wishes it not, to bear many disgraces, yielding to want, which truly teaches many lessons, to wit, falsehoods, deceits, and mischievous strifes, to a man even against his will: and they seem to him no evil, for it also breeds vexatious lack-of-means. But in poverty both the mean man, and he who is far better-born are seen, whensoever, I mean, want takes-hold-on-them. For the spirit of the former indulges in unjust thoughts, no, nor even is a right sentiment ever inherent in his breast: but the mind of the latter on-the-contrary follows neither bad nor good fortunes: it is right however that the bettermost man should have the courage to meet both the one and the other.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Respect your friends, and flee
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Respect your friends, and flee oaths that-ruin-men: but avoid, and give-heed-to, the wrath of immortals.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Make too much haste in
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Make too much haste in nothing: in all the works of man the-fitting-season is best: often a man, seeking gain, is hastening towards rank-and-honours, whom fortune readily draws astray into a great sin, and is wont to make him deem without difficulty that what is really evil, that is good: but that what is good-and-useful, that is bad.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Most dear though thou art
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Most dear though thou art, thou hast erred; and I, look you, am nowise to blame, but thou thyself hast chanced on sentiments not good.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: No treasure wilt thou lay
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: No treasure wilt thou lay up for thy children better than a sense-of-shame, which also, Cyrnus, attends good men.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Of no man, whom judgment
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Of no man, whom judgment and whom power attends, O Cyrnus, seem thou to be a worse companion.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: But when I drink, I
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: But when I drink, I am not about to become so drunk, nor does wine lead me on, so far as to speak a harsh word respecting you.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: None like me can I
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: None like me can I find, when I seek a trusty associate, in whom there is no guile. But when I have come to the touch-stone I am rubbed beside baser metal, as gold beside lead, and a mind of superiority is in me.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Many things pass me by
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Many things pass me by, even though I am conscious of them: but of necessity I am silent, knowing our power.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: To many men well-fitting doors
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: To many men well-fitting doors are not set on their tongue, and many things are a care to them, which should be uncared for. For oft that which is bad is better, if stored-up within, and good, having come abroad, is better than what is bad.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Of all things indeed to
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Of all things indeed to men on the earth, not to be born, and not to see the rays of the piercing sun, is best: but that when born he should, as soon as possible, cross the gates of Hades, and lie low, having heaped together for himself much earth.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: To beget and nurture a
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: To beget and nurture a child is easier than to implant right feelings: this at all events no one has yet contrived, in making the senseless sensible, and the mean noble; but if a god had granted this, I wot, to the sons of Æsculapius, to cure meanness, and the infatuated minds of men, many and great wages would they earn. And if mind were capable-of-being created and implanted in man, never would worthless son have been born, of worthy father, but he would have been heedful of prudent discourses. But by teaching you will never make the mean man noble.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: He is a fool, who
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: He is a fool, who has my mind indeed in safe-keeping, but pays no attention to his own proper mind.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: No one, look you, is
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: No one, look you, is in all things blest, but the nobler man has the heart to endure what is evil, and still is not known-to-all. But the baser man neither in woe nor weal knows how to remain in possession of spirit: the gifts of the gods come variously to mortals; yet it is right to have the courage to hold the gifts of the immortals, such as they give.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: If you choose to drench
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: If you choose to drench me, undefiled water shall flow ever clear from the top of my head: and you shall find me in all deeds like-as refined gold, ruddy to look-on, when rubbed by touch-stone; the colour of which from above the dark rust doth not touch, nor mould, but it has its brilliancy always pure.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: O man, hadst thou obtained
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: O man, hadst thou obtained a share of judgment, even as thou hast of folly, and hadst thou been sensible as thou art senseless, to many of these citizens thou wouldst appear an-object-of-envy, just as now thou art nothing-worth.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: A young woman, look you
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: A young woman, look you, is not an expedient thing for an old man: for she, like a light boat, does not heed the rudder, nor do anchors hold her: but, having burst her fastenings, oft in the nights she hath another harbour.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Never set thy mind at
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Never set thy mind at least on things impracticable, nor long for wealth, of which there is no accomplishment.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Easily, look you, the gods
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Easily, look you, the gods have given wealth, neither anything mean, nor noble: but there is glory attendant on a difficult work.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Practise yourself about virtue: and
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Practise yourself about virtue: and let what is just be dear to you, nor let gain, when it is base, get the upper hand of you.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Force no one of these
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Force no one of these against his will to remain with us, nor bid any, if he wishes it not, go out of doors. Nor rouse in-his-sleep, Simonides, whomsoever of us, drunken with wine, soft sleep shall have seized. Neither bid him that is watchful, sleep against his will, for every-thing-done-by-compulsion is vexatious. And to him that chooses to drink let one stand near and pour-out-wine: not every night does it happen to us to live delicately. Now I, for I have due measure of sweet wine, will go home, and be mindful of care-relaxing sleep; and I will show that wine is most pleasant for a man to drink, for neither am I a whit sober, nor yet am I very drunk. Now whoso exceeds the due measure of drinking, that man is no longer master of his tongue or mind: but he speaks scandalous words, which, to the sober, seem disgraceful, and nothing is he ashamed to do, whensoever he may be drunk. Though he were sensible before, then he is a fool: do you, then, knowing these things, not drink wine in excess; but either, before you are intoxicated, rise and go, lest your stomach constrain you, like a worthless hireling for-the-day; or be present, and do not drink: but you, though knowing these things, are ever babbling this foolish word, “pour-in: therefore, look you, you are drunk. For one cup is taken to friendship;” another is pledged: this you offer as a libation to the gods: the fourth you hold in your hand. And you know not how to say nay; now, look you, that man will be invincible, who, though he drink many cups, shall say nothing silly. But do ye discourse well, tarrying beside the bowl, long keeping-off contentions one from the other; speaking fairly and evenly alike to one and with all, and thus a banquet becomes not unpleasant.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Wine belongs to the senseless
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Wine belongs to the senseless man as well as the sensible. When, however, it is drunk above measure, it is wont to render the mind light.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: In fire, indeed, skilful men
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: In fire, indeed, skilful men try gold and silver, but wine is wont to show the mind of a man, even though he be exceeding sensible; wine which when drinking he is wont to praise beyond measure, so as to disgrace one being even wise aforetime.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: My head, Onomacritus, is heavy-with-wine
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: My head, Onomacritus, is heavy-with-wine, and wine does violence to me, but I am no longer master of my senses; nay, the chamber whirls-round. Come, let me rise and try whether perchance the wine hath my feet too, and my mind within my breast. I fear lest, in my drunkenness, I should do anything foolish, and incur a great disgrace.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Much wine drunk is bad
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Much wine drunk is bad: but if a man drink it with-judgment, ’tis not bad but good.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: So thou hast come, Clearistus
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: So thou hast come, Clearistus, after having accomplished passage across the deep sea, hither, wretched man, a beggar to a beggar. Under the ship’s sides, truly, we will place benches, Clearistus, such as we have, and as the gods give us: and we will supply the best of what we have: but should any one come, being a friend of thine, say to him, “Sit-at-meat, an thou lovest me.” I will neither set apart aught of my substance, nor, for the sake of entertaining thee, will we bring aught more from other quarters. Then should any inquire my means of subsistence, thus tell him, that I dive with difficulty as regards living well, but very well for one living with difficulty: so as not to fail even one guest of my father’s, though I am not able to afford feasts to more men.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Not to no purpose, Plutus
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Not to no purpose, Plutus, do mortals honour thee most, for of-a-truth thou bearest distress with ease. For verily it is fitting for the bettermost to have wealth indeed, but poverty is proper for a mean man to bear.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Alas me for youth and
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Alas me for youth and wretched old age, the latter coming on, and the former departing.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I have betrayed neither any
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I have betrayed neither any friend nor trusty comrade, nor is there aught servile in my spirit.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Ever is my heart cheered
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Ever is my heart cheered, whensoever I shall have heard the delightsome sound of vocal flutes. And I rejoice in drinking well, and in listing to a flute-player; I delight, too, in carrying the gay lyre in my hands.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Never is a slave’s head
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Never is a slave’s head erect, but always crooked, and has the neck askance. For neither from the squill do roses or hyacinths spring, no, nor ever from a bond-woman a free-spirited child.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: No man, dear Cyrnus, forges
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: No man, dear Cyrnus, forges fetters for himself, unless the gods beguile my judgment.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I fear, O son of
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I fear, O son of Polypas, lest insolence, even the insolence which destroyed the savage Centaurs, should ruin this state.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: ’Tis right that I, O
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: ’Tis right that I, O Cyrnus, should adjudicate this cause by rule and square, and deal fair play to both sides, namely, to oracular birds, and to burnt sacrifices, that so I may not incur the foul disgrace of error.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Never do violence to any
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Never do violence to any one through wickedness: for to the just man nought is better than good-conduct.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: A voiceless messenger stirs up
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: A voiceless messenger stirs up, O Cyrnus, war-of-many tears, seen clearly as it is from a conspicuous mountain-peak. Nay, then, place bridles on your swift-footed steeds, for methinks that they will encounter hostile men: nor long the way which they will traverse between us and the foe, unless the gods deceive my judgment.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: It behoves a man lying
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: It behoves a man lying in severe griefs to take heart, and to ask deliverance from them at the hands of the immortal gods.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Consider: the danger, look you
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Consider: the danger, look you, stands on a razor’s edge: at one moment you shall have much: at another far fewer possessions: so that you neither become exceeding rich in possessions, no, nor thrust yourself into much want-of-means.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Be it mine to have
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Be it mine to have somewhat myself, but to bestow the most of the riches of foes on my friends to enjoy.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Now ’tis meet that one
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Now ’tis meet that one should be invited to a banquet, and sit beside a worthy man, versed in all wisdom, so as to understand him whensoever he shall utter aught-of-wisdom, that so you may be instructed, and go home to your house with this gain.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Delighting myself in youth I
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Delighting myself in youth I sport-and-sing: for, when I have lost my life, I shall lie long beneath the earth, like a voiceless stone; and shall quit the delightful light of the sun, and, though I be a man-of-worth, yet shall see nothing any more.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Opinion, indeed, is a great
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Opinion, indeed, is a great evil to men, but experience a very excellent thing: many of the bettermost men have an opinion unproved-by-experience.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Do good, and good shall
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Do good, and good shall be done by you: but wherefore send you another messenger? the tidings of a benefit is easy.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: My friends abandon me, yes
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: My friends abandon me, yes, because I avoid my enemy, as pilot avoids the low-rocks in-the-sea.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: ’Tis easier to make a
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: ’Tis easier to make a mean man out of a bettermost man, than a noble man of a base: teach me not: I am not of an age to learn.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I hate a mean man
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I hate a mean man: and I veil myself when I approach him, having the volatile spirit of a little bird. I hate also a roaming woman, and a wanton man, who desires to plough the furrow of another. But the things which have gone by, it is impossible should become undone: the future, however, be that a care to our caution.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Danger, I wot, is attendant
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Danger, I wot, is attendant on all works, neither knoweth any one, when a matter begins, where he is likely to land. But the man who endeavours to be popular, without forethought, is wont to fall into great and severe ruin. Him however who doeth well is the deity that invests with everything, with lucky chances, and riddance from folly.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: It is right to endure
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: It is right to endure what the gods give to men, and to bear easily the lot of both classes. Neither when distressed with ills be vexed at heart, nor be delighted on a sudden with good fortune, before you have seen the extreme end.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Goud Sir, let us be
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Goud Sir, let us be companions one to another at a distance. There is satiety of everything save wealth. Long then let us be even friends; but do thou associate with other men also, who better know thy mind.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: You have not escaped-my-notice as
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: You have not escaped-my-notice as you walked along the road, on which even aforetime you used to drive, stealing my friendship. Away with you, hateful to gods, and faithless to men, you who had in your bosom a chilly spotted snake.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Such-like deeds, such insolence, ruined
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Such-like deeds, such insolence, ruined the Magnesians also, as now possesses this sacred city.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Fulness hath ere now destroyed
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Fulness hath ere now destroyed far more men, look you, than famine, to wit, as many as were desirous of having more than their share.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: At the beginning a lie
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: At the beginning a lie gets small thanks, but at last base lucre, in truth, and ill arise, both of them: nor is there anything noble to any man, whom a lie attends, even though it be the first that has gone forth from his mouth.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: It is not hard to
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: It is not hard to blame one’s neighbour, no, nor to praise him: these things are a care to mean men. And mean men do not choose to be silent, prating mischief rather, but the noble know how to preserve moderation in all things.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: No one of the present
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: No one of the present race of men doth the sun look down upon, being entirely good and moderate.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Not to any great extent
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Not to any great extent are all things accomplished to men’s liking, for immortals are far-superior to mortals.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I am much tost-about in
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I am much tost-about in difficulties, being vexed at heart: for we have not outrun extreme poverty.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Every one honours a rich
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Every one honours a rich man, but dishonours a poor: and in all men there is the same mind.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: All-kinds-of-baseness exist among men, and
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: All-kinds-of-baseness exist among men, and all-kinds-of excellence, and devices for livelihood.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: ’Tis hard for a sensible
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: ’Tis hard for a sensible man to speak much among the senseless, and so it is always to be silent: for this is impossible.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: In truth, ’tis disgraceful for
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: In truth, ’tis disgraceful for a drunken man to be amongst sober men: and disgraceful if a sober man remains among the drunken.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Man’s-estate and youth lighten a
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Man’s-estate and youth lighten a man’s mind, and stir up the spirits of many to error.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Whoso hath not a mind
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Whoso hath not a mind that is master of his inclinations, he, I wot, Cyrnus, lies ever in follies, and in great errors.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Consult twice and thrice on
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Consult twice and thrice on whatever shall have come into your mind, for a hasty man, look you, is hurried-to-ruin.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Judgment and sense-of-shame attend men
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Judgment and sense-of-shame attend men that are good, who now are really few among the many.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Hope and hazard are alike
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Hope and hazard are alike among men: for both these are severe deities.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Often beyond both expectation and
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Often beyond both expectation and hope it is given men to discover the works of men, but success is not wont to follow their counsels.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: A single individual, look you
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: A single individual, look you, troubles neither one-well-affected, nor his foe, unless he meet with a serious matter. Many are friends and comrades over the bowl, but fewer in a serious matter.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Few companions would you find
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Few companions would you find faithful protectors, when you are placed in great perplexity of spirit.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Now at length a sense-of-shame
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Now at length a sense-of-shame hath perished among mankind, but shamelessness roams over the earth.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Thou luckless poverty, why, seated
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Thou luckless poverty, why, seated on my shoulders, dost thou disgrace my body and mind? Nay, thou teachest me against my will perforce many disgraceful arts, though I know from men good and noble lessons.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: May I be fortunate, and
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: May I be fortunate, and dear to the immortal gods, O Cyrnus; then am I eager for no other excellence.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Along with thee, Cyrnus, when
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Along with thee, Cyrnus, when thou hast suffered misfortune, we are all distrest: but of-a-truth grief for another lasts but-for-a-day.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: In hard fortunes be not
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: In hard fortunes be not at all excessively disgusted at heart, neither rejoice in prosperity: for ’tis a noble man’s course to bear all things.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Nor is it right to
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Nor is it right to swear this, “that this thing shall never be,” for the gods also, in whose hands is the issue, are wroth.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Yet still one ought to
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Yet still one ought to do somewhat: both good hath arisen from ill, and ill from good; ay, and the poor man very quickly becomes rich, while he who has possessed very much on a sudden is wont to lose everything, in fact, in a single night. And sensible man errs, and glory oft attends a senseless man: honour too even a mean man is wont to obtain.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: If I had wealth, Simonides
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: If I had wealth, Simonides, even such as I was acquainted with, I should not be vexed at associating with the noble.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: But now they (riches) pass-me-by
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: But now they (riches) pass-me-by, though I knew them, and I am mute through poverty, though still knowing better than many. Wherefore we are borne-on now, having pulled down our white sails, from the Melian Sea, through murky gloom: but they do not choose to bale the ship, and the sea surmounts both the vessel’s sides, whereby with great difficulty any one saves himself: yet the sailors are slumbering, and have made the pilot, good though he was, cease from his work, the pilot who used to watch over it understandingly. By force they plunder property, order is upset, and no longer is there an equal distribution in common: but the porters bear-rule, and the mean are above the noble. I fear lest haply the waves should ingulf the ship. Let thus much have been wrapt in riddles darkly, for the men-of-worth; but a man, if he be wise, would be cognizant also of the evil.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Many dunces have riches, but
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Many dunces have riches, but others seek what is noble. though harassed by severe poverty: but impossibility-of-working lies-beside both: the one class want-of-riches impedes, of-intellect the other.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: ’Tis impossible for mortals to
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: ’Tis impossible for mortals to strive against immortals or to deal out justice. To none is this permitted.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: It is not right to
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: It is not right to cherish what should not be cherished, nor to do what it were better to leave unaccomplished.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: With satisfaction mayest thou duly
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: With satisfaction mayest thou duly perform thy voyage through the great sea, and may Neptune bring thee home, a joy to thy friends.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Many men, look you, being
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Many men, look you, being senseless, has fulness ruined, for ’tis hard to understand moderation, when good things are present.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: In truth, O my spirit
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: In truth, O my spirit, I cannot afford thee all things fitting. Bear up: for not by any means thou alone art fond of what is beautiful.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: When I am flourishing, friends
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: When I am flourishing, friends are many; but should any calamity have chanced upon me, few retain a faithful spirit. For to the multitude of men there is this virtue only, namely, to be rich: but of the rest, I wot, there is no use.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Not even though you should
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Not even though you should have the sense of Rhadamanthus himself, and be more knowing than Sisyphus, son of Æolus; (even he who by his cunning came-up-again from Hades, after having persuaded Proserpine by wily words, Proserpine, who gives oblivion to mortals, and misleads their mind: and never hath any other devised this, I ween, whomsoever in truth the black mist of death has enshrouded, and he has come to the chilly place of the dead, and crossed the dark portals which confine the souls of the dead, even though they refuse: yet, verily, even thence came back the hero Sisyphus to the light of the sun through his own exceeding-shrewdness;) nor if you could make falsehoods like to truths, having the skilful tongue of the god-like Nestor, and were swifter of foot than the fleet Harpies, and the sons of Boreas, whose feet go swiftly. Nay, then, ’tis right that all should lay up this maxim, that wealth has the most power among all.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Equally rich, look you, are
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Equally rich, look you, are he to whom there is much silver and gold, and plains of wheat-producing earth, horses and mules; and he to whom that which is needful is ready, so that he may enjoy himself in pleasures of stomach, sides, and feet; and boys and women: for when the fitting season of these shall have arrived, and at-the-same-time their youthful prime is suitable, these are wealth to mortals: for no one goes to Hades with all his immense wealth. Neither by paying ransom can he escape death, or heavy diseases, or wretched old age coming upon him.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: O Father Jove, would that
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: O Father Jove, would that it might please the gods, that their insolence should delight sinners; and that this might be agreeable to their mind, namely, that whoso ruthlessly works daring deeds in his heart, nowise standing-in-awe-of the gods, that he, I say, thereafter should atone for his evil deeds; and that the father’s infatuation should not in after-time be a woe to the children. But that children, who, being born of an unjust sire, know and do justice, reverencing thy wrath, O son of Cronus, and from the very first loving the right amongst the citizens, should not pay the penalty for any transgression of their sires. May these things be agreeable to the blessed gods: but now he that commits wicked deeds escapes, and another presently suffers the punishment. Then how, O king of immortals, is it just, that whoso is aloof from unrighteous deeds, holding no transgression, nor sinful oath, but being righteous, should suffer what is not just? What other mortal, too, I pray, when he looks at this man, would afterwards stand-in-awe-of the gods, and entertaining what feeling? When an unrighteous, infatuated man, having avoided the wrath neither of any man nor of the immortals in anywise, doeth wrongs, and is glutted with wealth; whereas the righteous are wasted, being worn out by severe poverty.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Having learned this, dear comrade
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Having learned this, dear comrade, get riches justly, keeping a prudent spirit, afar from blind-folly, and ever remembering these my words; then at the last you will commend me, giving heed to a wise speech.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: May Jove, dwelling in heaven
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: May Jove, dwelling in heaven, hold on high his right hand ever over this city for its health and safety, as well as the other immortal blessed gods; but may Apollo nerve my tongue and mind: and on the other hand let the holy melody sound with lyre, and also flute; but let us, having made full drink-offerings to the gods, drink and speak pleasantly one with the other, in no wise fearing the war of the Medes. So be it; and better still be it ours, enjoying a cheerful spirit, aloof from cares to pass our days cheerily, and delight ourselves, and to drive far away ill fates, wretched age, and the end of death.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: ’Tis meet that the Muses’
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: ’Tis meet that the Muses’ servant and messenger, if he know aught special of wisdom, should not begrudge it: but should seek after some things, point out some, and invent others; alone knowing for what purpose he should use them.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: O sovereign Phœbus, thou thyself
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: O sovereign Phœbus, thou thyself fencedst the citadel in favour to Alcathous, son of Pelops; do thou then ward off from this city the insolent army of Medes, that so thy people, in cheerfulness, as spring comes on, may send thee splendid hecatombs, delighting themselves with lyre, and lovely festival, with choirs of pæans, and shoutings around thine altar. For of a truth I fear, when I look on the folly and people-destroying seditions of the Greeks. Yet do thou, Phœbus, propitiously guard this our city. For I have gone aforetime both to the Sicilian land, and I have gone to Eubœa’s vine-clad plain, and to Sparta, splendid city of reed-nursing Eurotas, and all did with alacrity entreat-me-kindly when I came. But no pleasure in them came over my spirit; so much, I wot, is nought else dearer than our father-land.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Never may other fresher care
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Never may other fresher care present itself to me, in place of charming wisdom; but may I ever, possessing this, delight myself with lyre, with dance, and song; and with these blessings may I have a noble mind.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Harming by baneful deeds neither
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Harming by baneful deeds neither any stranger nor any of your townsmen, but, being just, delight your own mind: and of the unfeeling citizens some will speak ill of you, others better. The noble one man blames much: another praises: but of the mean there is no record: but of men unblamed is none upon the earth; and ’tis best for him, of whom there is no care to the greater number.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: No one of men will
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: No one of men will either be, or hath been, born, who will go down to Hades pleasing to all. For not even he who reigns over mortals and immortals, Jove, son of Cronus, can please all mortals.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: It behoves, indeed, a man
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: It behoves, indeed, a man that goeth-to-consult-the oracle, Cyrnus, to keep more straightly than compasses, line, or rule; such a man, I mean, as he to whom the god at Pytho, having given answer to the priestess, shall have indicated a prophecy from his rich sanctuary; for neither though you add aught would you discover any remedy, nor if you have diminished aught, would you escape the punishment of offence, on the part of the gods.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I have experienced a thing
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I have experienced a thing nowise inferior to an unseemly death, but of all other things most vexatious, Cyrnus. My friends have cast me off: so I, having drawn near to mine enemies, am about to see also what mind they have.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: An ox, stamping on my
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: An ox, stamping on my tongue with sturdy foot, restrains me from chattering, though I am versed in it, Cyrnus. But still it is impossible to escape from what is fated to suffer; and what I am fated to suffer I nowise fear to endure. Into a vast unspeakable evil are we come, wherein above all, O Cyrnus, the fate of death may seize us both together.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: But they who dishonour their
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: But they who dishonour their parents, when growing old, for these, Cyrnus, there is no place of esteem.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Neither aid any tyrant in
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Neither aid any tyrant in the hopes that ’tis matter of gain, nor slay him, when you have entered into covenants sworn before the gods.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: How hath our spirit had
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: How hath our spirit had the heart to sing to the flute-player? but from the forum is seen the limit of the land, which maintains with her fruits men wearing at feasts and on auburn locks purple garlands. Nay, come now, Scythian, shave thy hair, and cease from revelling, and lament the fragrant country lost.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: By faith have I lost
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: By faith have I lost wealth, and by unbelief preserved it: but the counsel of both is difficult. All this my property is with the crows and in ruin; nor is any of the immortal blessed gods to blame in my judgment: but man’s violence, and much gain, and wrong have thrust me out of many good things into poverty.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: There are two fates truly
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: There are two fates truly of drinking to wretched mortals, limb-relaxing thirst, and baneful drunkenness. Now between these I shall abide, nor will you persuade me either not to drink at all, or to be excessively drunken. Wine, indeed, in other respects is agreeable to me, but in one ’tis disagreeable, to wit, when, having made me drunk, it leads me against a foe. But when one, being properly above, shall have been lowered, then ’tis meet he should go home, having ceased from drinking.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: To upset a man well
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: To upset a man well established is easy; but to set right that which is ill settled, is difficult.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Spurn the empty-spirited rabble, strike
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Spurn the empty-spirited rabble, strike them with sharp goad, and place around them a galling yoke. For no more will you find a populace so fond of despots, among all men, as many as the sun looks down upon.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: May Olympian Jove destroy the
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: May Olympian Jove destroy the man who chooses to deceive his comrade, prating smoothly to him. I knew indeed even before, but much better now, that the mean have no gratitude.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Oft hath this city through
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Oft hath this city through the baseness of its rulers, like a ship wandering out of its course, driven past the land.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: But if any of my
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: But if any of my friends sees me in any trouble, turning his head away, he does not even choose to look on me; yet if any good comes to me from any quarter, such as often happen to a man, I find many greetings and friendships.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: My friends forsake me, and
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: My friends forsake me, and will not give me aught, when men appear: but I of-my-own-accord go out at-eve, and come-in again at dawn, when the voice of wakening cocks is heard.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: To many useless men the
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: To many useless men the god gives good wealth, which being nothing, is better neither to itself nor its friends. But the great glory of martial excellence will never perish, for a warrior saves both country and city.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Then may the broad brazen
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Then may the broad brazen vault-of-heaven fall on me from above, that terror of men of olden-time, if I shall not help them indeed who love me: but be to my foes a vexation and great source-of-loss.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Wine, I in part commend
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Wine, I in part commend thee, partly blame: neither can I wholly either ever hate or love thee. Good art thou, and bad. Nay, who would blame thee or who praise thee, if he has due measure of wisdom?

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Drink wine, which to me
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Drink wine, which to me from the top of Taygetus vines have borne, which the old man, beloved by the gods, Theotimus, planted in the mountain glades, introducing cold water from the grove-of-plane-trees. Drinking of which, thou wilt dispel harsh cares, and when thou hast well drunk, wilt be far the lighter.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: May peace and wealth possess
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: May peace and wealth possess the state, that I may revel with others, for I love not baneful war. Neither do thou too much lend an ear, when the herald shouts loud and far: for we are not fighting for our father-land. Yet ’tis disgraceful, when present and mounted on fleet-footed steeds, not to look upon tearful war.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Alas me, for our cowardice
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Alas me, for our cowardice Cerinthus is undone, and the goodly vineyard of Lelantum is stript. The noble flee; the mean administer the state: would Jove might destroy the Cypselizing race!

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Nought better than judgment hath
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Nought better than judgment hath a man in himself, I wot, or more vexatious, Cyrnus, than lack-of-judgment.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Cyrnus, be not in all
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
