poems.text: Cyrnus, be not in all respects wroth with mortal men, knowing that you have a mind, like as each man has, in your breast, and deeds also. To mortals; whether the just man, or the unjust, great loss may ensue. Of each man one act is worse, another better: but no man is himself wise in all respects.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Whoso watches expenditure, hunting after
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Whoso watches expenditure, hunting after riches, has the most distinguished excellence in the sight of men-of-understanding.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: For if it were possible
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: For if it were possible to ascertain the end of life, to wit, how much time having accomplished, a man were fated to go to Hades, it would be reasonable that he, who awaited his destiny the longer time, should most spare the substance which he had. But now ’tis not so: a circumstance which really rouses great vexation in me, and I am heart-worn, and have my mind in doubt. So I stand in a cross-road, and there are two roads in front for me: I consider on which of these I am to proceed first: either being at no expense I waste my life in wretchedness; or, accomplishing but few works, I live pleasantly. For I, too, have seen a man who was careful, and never would allow his stomach food fit for a free man, rich though he was: yet ere he had finished he descended within Pluto’s mansion, and the chance-comer from among men received his wealth; so that he toiled in vain and did not give as a man could wish. Another have I seen, who indulging his appetites squandered his wealth, and said, “I delight my soul, and then retire:” but he begs of all his friends, wheresoever he may have seen one. Thus, Damocles, ’tis best of all to regulate your expenditure according to your means, and to pay attention to this; for neither will you then toil first, and give another a share in the fruit of your toil; nor will you finish your servitude a beggar; no, nor, should old age come, will all your wealth flee-away: for in such a class as this ’tis best to have riches: since if you are rich, you will have many friends; but should you be poor, then few: and then no longer is the same man equally good.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: ’Tis best to spare: since
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: ’Tis best to spare: since not even does any one wail for the dead, unless he sees wealth left behind.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Few among men doth worth
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Few among men doth worth and beauty attend: happy he who hath obtained both of these: all honour him: the young alike, and his equals-in-age, and his elders give place to him.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I cannot sing tunefully with
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I cannot sing tunefully with my voice, like a nightingale, for the last night I went to a revel. Nor do I set up the piper as an excuse; but a comrade, no wise lacking sense, fails me. Close to the piper will I sing, standing here on the right, and praying to the immortal gods.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I will walk by rule
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I will walk by rule on the straight path, swerving to neither side: for ’tis meet I should entertain all right views. I will distinguish my bright native-city, neither having brought myself under the power of the commonalty, nor complying with unjust men.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Though having overtaken with my
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Though having overtaken with my feet, as a lion trusting in his strength, a fawn from a stag, yet have I not drunk its blood: and though I have mounted lofty walls, I have not sacked the city; though I have yoked my steeds, I have not set foot in my chariot. I have accomplished and yet not accomplished, succeeded and yet not succeeded, done yet not done, achieved yet not achieved.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: There are two evils to
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: There are two evils to him that doth good to the mean man: he will both be stript of his own many possessions, and get no thanks.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: If, after having experienced some
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: If, after having experienced some great good from me, you are not thankful, may you come again a beggar to my house.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: While I was drinking alone
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: While I was drinking alone of the dark-water spring, methought the water was of a sweet and limpid nature; but now hath it been polluted; water is mixt with water: I will drink then of other fountain or river.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Never praise before that you
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Never praise before that you shall have clearly known as to a man, the temper, disposition, bent, which he is of. Many, look you, having a base and wily nature, hide having put on themselves a spirit to-last-the-day, but of each of all these time discloses the character: for I too, I wot, have gone far wide of my judgment, and have been before-hand in praising you, ere I had thoroughly learned your character: but now at length, as a ship, I stand far apart.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: But what excellence is it
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: But what excellence is it to drink and carry off the prize of wine? oft verily even the worthless man surpasses the worthy.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: There is no one of
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: There is no one of mortals, who, when once earth shall cover him, and he shall have descended to Erebus and the abode of Proserpine, delights therein, because he neither hears lyre nor piper, nor lifts to his lips the gifts of Bacchus. Seeing these things, I shall feel well at heart, so long as untremblingly I carry light limbs and head.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Be no man friend to
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Be no man friend to me in tongue, but in deed too: and let him be active both with hands and means. Neither let him delight my spirit with words over cups, but show by acts if he can do aught good.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Let us then stake our
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Let us then stake our dear spirits on festivals, while yet they can bear the delightsome works of enjoyment. For quickly as thought passes brilliant youth, neither is the speed of coursers fleeter, even those which impetuously bear a spear-brandishing warrior to the struggle of men, whilst they exult in the wheat-bearing plain.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Drink when men drink: but
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Drink when men drink: but when thou shalt have been at-all disgusted in spirit, let no man know that thou art troubled. One while, look you, you will grieve at suffering, and at another, doing, you are able to rejoice, and at different times you are a different man.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Would it was allowed, Academus
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Would it was allowed, Academus, that thou shouldst chant a lovely hymn, and that a slave in the fair flower of youth might be the prize proposed to thee and me contending on the score of skill—then shouldst thou know how much better are mules than asses.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: But when the sun indeed
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: But when the sun indeed just now cheers on his solid-hoofed steeds in ether, holding the middle of the day, then cease we from dinner, to go whither inclination leads every one, gratifying the appetite with all manner of good things. and let a comely Lacedæmonian maiden with slender hands quickly bring out water, and carry in the garlands.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: But excellence, this is the
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: But excellence, this is the noblest prize among men, and the most fair for a wise man to bear off; and this is a common blessing to every city and people, he who with-broad-stride stands fast amid the first ranks.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Now I will counsel men
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Now I will counsel men for their-common-good, that every one enjoying the bright bloom of youth may also entertain sound thoughts in his heart, to enjoy the good, each of his own possessions: for twice to grow-young is not given by the gods, neither is there to mortal men an escape from death: but baneful and destructive old age overpowers them, and touches the tops of their heads.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: How blest and fortunate and
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: How blest and fortunate and lucky he, who hath descended to Hades dark mansion, without having experienced troubles, before that he has made his enemies cower, and overcome them even perforce, and ascertained what spirit his friends have.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Straightway perspiration without measure flows
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Straightway perspiration without measure flows down my skin, and I am fluttered when I look at the prime of my equals-in-age, delightsome alike and beautiful; for it ought to be of longer duration, but, like a dream, precious youth is a short-lived thing: and presently over-head hangs unhappy and unsightly old age.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Never will I place my
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Never will I place my neck under the galling yoke of my enemies, not even though Tmolus is above my head.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: To the meaner sort their
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: To the meaner sort their minds are more empty through baseness: but the doings of the noble are always more direct.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: The practice of mischief, look
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: The practice of mischief, look you, among men is easy: but the method of good, Cyrnus, is difficult.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Take courage, mine heart, in
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Take courage, mine heart, in troubles, e’en though you have suffered things unendurable: the heart of the baser sort, look you, is ever too hasty. Neither do you, at any rate, aggravating your chagrin at works that-have-been-unaccomplished, bear hate, nor be indignant: neither vex your friends. Nor delight your enemies: for the destined awards of the gods not easily could mortal man escape, either if he descended to the bottom of the dark lake, or when murky Tartarus holds him.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: To beguile a noble man
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: To beguile a noble man, look you, is most difficult, as it hath long been decided, Cyrnus, in my judgment. I knew it indeed even before, but much better now; that the mean have no gratitude.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Senseless and fools are the
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Senseless and fools are the men who drink not wine when the dog-star rises. Come hither, with the aid of the piper let us laugh and drink beside one that weeps, whilst we delight in his griefs. Let us sleep: and the watching over the city shall be the warder’s care, the watch over our lovely rockless fatherland. Yes, by Jove, if any of these sleeps even wrapped-up, he will listen to our revelling eagerly. Now let us drink and enjoy ourselves, speaking fairly: and what shall be hereafter, that is the gods’ concern.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: To you now, as to
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: To you now, as to a dear child, I myself will give sound advice; and do you ponder these things in your heart and mind. Never do any evil hastily, but deliberate in the deep of your heart, and with your better mind. For of them that contend, ’tis the heart and the mind that contend; but counsel leads to a good and sound mind.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: But this account we will
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: But this account we will let-pass. Do thou however pipe to me: and both of us will be mindful of the Muses. For they have given these delightful gifts to-hold, to thee, and me, and in truth to the dwellers-all-around.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Timagoras, ’tis hard for one-seeing-from-far
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Timagoras, ’tis hard for one-seeing-from-far, to understand the temper of many, even though he be wise. For some have meanness disguised by riches; and others rank by ruinous poverty.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: But in youth ’tis best
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: But in youth ’tis best to sleep beside an equal-in-age, satisfying the desire of works of-love: ’tis better too to sing with a piper accompanying you, when you go a revelling: than this nought, look you, else is more delightsome to men and women. What to me are riches and dignity? Delight along with good cheer surpasses everything.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Senseless and childish are the
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Senseless and childish are the men, who mourn for the dead, and not the flower of manhood, when it perishes.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Prithee, delight thyself, dear heart
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Prithee, delight thyself, dear heart: soon will there be some other men, and I in death shall be black earth.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Cyrnus, direct a various temper-of-mind
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Cyrnus, direct a various temper-of-mind towards all your friends, mingling such a character as each is of. One while follow this character; at another be diverse in your nature: a better thing, look you, is wisdom than great excellence. Of a thing unaccomplished ’tis most hard to know the end, how the god will accomplish this. For gloom is spread over, and previous to that which is about to be, the bounds of human helplessness are not to-be-understood.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: No one of mine enemies
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: No one of mine enemies will I blame, if he be noble; no, nor will I commend a friend, if he be a mean man.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Thus it behoves the well-born
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Thus it behoves the well-born man, I wot, directing his thoughts to it, to keep them ever stedfast until the end to a friend. You needs must bear worthily many unpleasant things, since you know not how to do that which is not pleasant to yourself. Castor and Pollux, ye who dwell in divine Lacedæmon on the Eurotas, beautifully-flowing stream, if ever I should devise evil for a friend, may I myself find it: but should he devise aught against me, may he find twice as much.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: My mind is distressed respecting
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: My mind is distressed respecting your friendship: for I can neither love nor hate you: knowing as I do that ’tis hard to hate, after one has been a friend to a man; and hard to love a man without his concurrence. Look therefore now to another; to me at least there was no constraint to do this: namely, the kindnesses, for which aforetime you were grateful to me.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Now even on wings am
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Now even on wings am I uplifted, like a bird from a vast marsh, having escaped from a base man, and having dragged away my neck. But you, when you have lost my friendship, will afterwards be sensible of my prudence, no matter who it was that counselled you concerning me, and bade you go away and abandon my friendship.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Insolence hath ruined both the
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Insolence hath ruined both the Magnesians, and Colophon, and Smyrna: Cyrnus, it will certainly ruin us likewise. But having been put to the test, and being rubbed beside lead, as being refined gold, you will be fair to all.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Ah wretched me for now
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Ah wretched me for now have I become a laughing-stock to foes, and to my friends a trouble, having suffered sadly.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: O Cyrnus, they who were
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: O Cyrnus, they who were noble aforetime, are now on the other hand mean: and those who were base before, are now noble: who can endure to look upon these things, to wit, the noble more dishonoured, and the baser sort obtaining honour? whilst the well-born man espouses a wile from a mean man’s house. So deceiving each other they exult one over the other, cherishing remembrance neither of good nor bad.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Possessing riches, you have reproached
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Possessing riches, you have reproached me with poverty: but something I have, and something more I shall make, after having paid my vows to the gods.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: O wealth, of all gods
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: O wealth, of all gods fairest and most delightsome, with thy aid, e’en though mean, I become a noble man.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: May I have youth’s prime
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: May I have youth’s prime, and may Latona’s son, Phœbus Apollo, love me, and Jove, sovereign of immortals; that so I may live my life aloof from all ills, delighting my spirit with youth and riches.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Remind me not of ills
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Remind me not of ills: I have suffered, look you, such treatment as Ulysses; who went to the vast mansion of Hades, and came up again from it; Ulysses, who, prudent as in truth he was, also slew with pitiless steel the suitors of Penelope, his wedded spouse: she who had long awaited him, while she remained abiding beside his dear son, until he set foot in the land, and trod the terror-causing inmost corners.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: If I but drink, I
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: If I but drink, I care not for spirit-wasting poverty, nor hostile men, who speak ill of me. But I lament for delightsome youth, which is failing me: and I bewail troublesome old-age coming-upon-me.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Cyrnus, for present friends we
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Cyrnus, for present friends we will stay the beginning of ill: and let us seek remedies for the growing wound.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Hope alone remains, a kind
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Hope alone remains, a kind goddess among mortals, the rest have abandoned us, and gone to Olympus.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Gone is Faith, a mighty
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Gone is Faith, a mighty goddess: gone from men Temperance: the Graces too, my friend, have quitted earth, and just oaths are no more to be relied on among men, neither does any-one reverence the immortal gods. But the race of holy men hath waned, nor are they any longer sensible of ordinances, no, nor holy lives. Yet so long as a man lives, and beholds the light of the sun, acting-piously as regards the gods, let him wait on Hope. And let him pray to the gods, burning also splendid thighs of victims, and to Hope let him sacrifice first and last. And let him ever muse on the perverted language of unjust men, who, nowise reverencing the immortal gods, are ever setting their thoughts on the possessions of others, having attached shameful marks to evil deeds.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Never let go your present
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Never let go your present friend, and seek out another, complying with the words of meaner men.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Be it mine to be
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Be it mine to be rich, aloof from evil cares, and to live harmlessly, meeting-with no ill.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I neither long nor pray
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I neither long nor pray to be rich; but be it mine to live on my little store, and find no hurt.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Wealth and wisdom are a
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Wealth and wisdom are a matter most irresistible ever; for neither could you over-fill the desire with wealth: and in like manner the wisest man doth not shun wisdom, but longs after it: yet cannot satisfy his desire therewith.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: No treasure is it better
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: No treasure is it better to lay-up-for your children; yet give it, Cyrnus, to noble men when they crave it. For no man is in all respects all-blessed: but the noble man has resolution to keep his misfortune, albeit not manifest to all, whilst the meaner person knows not how to keep his spirit even alike, in prosperity or in adversity. But on mortals fall various behests of the immortals; to endure then the gifts of the immortals, such as they give men to have, it is meet.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: In prudent men, eyes, tongue
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: In prudent men, eyes, tongue, and ears, and man’s intelligence are-by-nature in the midst of their breasts.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Company with the noble: but
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Company with the noble: but never follow the base, whensoever you are finishing a journey or your traffic. Of the noble noble is the answer, noble the works: but of the baser sort the winds carry away the worthless words. From evil-company come ills: and well wilt thou too understand this, since thou hast erred against the mighty immortals.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: The gods, O Cyrnus, give
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: The gods, O Cyrnus, give judgment as the best boon to mortals: judgment hath the issues of every man. O happy he that truly hath it in his mind. Verily it is far superior to dangerous insolence and wretched satiety. But satiety is an evil to mortals: than which two nought is more evil; for all mischief, Cyrnus, is from these.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Would that, O Cyrnus, thou
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Would that, O Cyrnus, thou mightest be clear from suffering and doing disgraceful deeds; then wouldst thou have greatest experience in virtue.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Cyrnus, reverence and fear the
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Cyrnus, reverence and fear the gods; for this prevents man either from doing or saying unholy things.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: To lay-low a tyrant that
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: To lay-low a tyrant that grindeth-down-his-people, even as you will, is no call for wrath on the part of the gods.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Good sense and good speech
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Good sense and good speech, these things are-by-nature in but few men, who are masters of both these.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: No one by paying ransom
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: No one by paying ransom can escape death or severe misfortune, unless fate impose an issue. Neither can mortal man, though he wish it, by gifts escape anxieties, to wit, when the god sends griefs.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I desire not to lie
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I desire not to lie in regal couch when dead; but be mine some good thing whilst I am yet alive. Prickles, I ween, to a dead man are a like couch to embroidered carpets; the wood is either hard or soft: matters not.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Neither swear by the gods
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Neither swear by the gods a perjured oath, for it is not endurable to hide from the immortals a debt that is due.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I hear, son of Polypas
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I hear, son of Polypas, the voice of the shrill-crying crane, even her, who to mortals comes as harbinger of the season for ploughing; and it smote my dark heart that others possess my flourishing fields, neither do my mules drag the bent-yoke of the plough, on account of that ever-to-be-remembered voyage.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I will not go, neither
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I will not go, neither shall a tyrant be lamented by me, nor go beneath the earth with wailing over his tomb. No, nor would he, if I were dead, either be grieved, or let fall warm tears adown his eyes.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: I neither forbid you, nor
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: I neither forbid you, nor invite you, to revel: you will be troublesome, when present, and friendly, whensoever you are absent.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Never let us sit down
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Never let us sit down and laugh beside them that mourn, O Cyrnus, delighting ourselves in our own advantages.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: To deceive an enemy, indeed
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: To deceive an enemy, indeed, and ill-affected man, is hard, Cyrnus: but for a friend to deceive a friend is easy.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Nothing, Cyrnus, is more sweet
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Nothing, Cyrnus, is more sweet than a good wife: I am witness, and be thou so to me of my truthfulness.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Speech is wont to bring
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Speech is wont to bring many false-steps to mortal men, when the judgment, Cyrnus, is disturbed.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: The cares of men have
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: The cares of men have had allotted to them, and possess, various wings, being divided for the sake of spirit and subsistence.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: Be young, dear heart: soon
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: Be young, dear heart: soon will there be some other men; and I, having died, shall be dark earth.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: But growing old, he is
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: But growing old, he is distinguished among the citizens, nor does any wish to hurt him, in point of respect or justice.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: On no one, Cyrnus, do
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: On no one, Cyrnus, do the rays of the sun that-giveth-light-to-men look down, over whom blame doth not hang.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: But I am not able
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: But I am not able to ascertain what mind the citizens entertain, for neither when I do good nor ill do I satisfy them.

poems.title: Maxims of Theognis: For heretofore hath a marine
poems.author: Theognis of Megara
poems.note: Literal prose translation by the Rev. J. Banks (Bohn, 1856), printed as prose: the plain-sense companion to Frere’s verse version. Banks’s hyphenated compounds are his own.
poems.text: For heretofore hath a marine corpse invited me home, though dead, yet speaking with living voice.
